headline: Iradenergo to study 2 MW floating solar at Kyzyl-Adyr; winter peak stays with Toktogul
dek: A donor fund will pay about US$350,000 for the feasibility study, but no pilot cost, contract or loan has been published and irrigators have yet to be asked.
paragraphs: Iradenergo said on Tuesday that it will study a floating solar array on the Kyzyl-Adyr Reservoir in Kara-Buura District, with a donor fund paying about US$350,000 (IS 2.94 million at the official rate of 8.40) for the feasibility study. The working idea is a pilot of around 2 MW on the water, with the state utility buying the output as it already buys from the Talas Solar Park on the Boz-Tektir terrace.

The company's spokesman, Vladislav Ten, was careful about what the array would and would not do. "It is a study, and it is a midday source," he said. "It adds nothing between 18:00 and 22:00, and that is the winter peak. Toktogul and the Naryn cascade carry the peak, and they will go on carrying it." Panels produce nothing after dark, and in November the evening peak falls well after sunset.

Toktogul itself is also ruled out for the idea. Mr Ten said the reservoir's level swings with the winter drawdown are too deep to float panels on. The Toktogul reservoir held 15.31 cubic kilometres of its 19 this morning, 80.6% full and falling by 58 million cubic metres in a day. It stood at 81.5% on Tuesday, the day Iradenergo made its announcement.

The company has not published what the pilot would cost, who would build it or how it would be financed. The donor money covers the study only. Asked whether Iradenergo would borrow for the array or ask the budget for it, Mr Ten said those questions "come after the study, not before". No construction contract has been listed on the State Procurement Portal.

The reservoir belongs to the irrigation system first. Bermet Asylova, a hydrologist at Talas State University, said covering part of the surface could cut evaporation, which is the usual argument for floating panels. She said the answer depends on how much of the surface is covered and on how far the level moves when farms draw water in summer. "The swing at Kyzyl-Adyr is far smaller than at Toktogul, but it is not nothing," she said. "The anchoring has to follow the water, and someone has to check what winter ice does to it." The Ministry of Agriculture and Water Resources and the Talas basin irrigators must agree on water use before anything is built. The ministry had not replied to the Herald's questions by the time of going to press.

In the valley the question is more practical. Marat Usupov, 58, who runs a tyre shop on the Trans-Talas road and keeps two horses at the Hippodrome stables, buys about 60 bales of hay each autumn, and said the bale price follows the canal water. "Hay was 26 som a bale in the valleys this month," he said. "If panels help the reservoir keep its water, good. If they get in the way of the rota, the farmers will say so before the engineers do."

Jyrgalbek Osmonaliev, head of the Kara-Buura District administration, welcomed the study. He said the district would like to see the reservoir used for more than irrigation, and that the array would sit next to the existing grid line, which Iradenergo cites as one advantage of the site. He did not say whether the district would offer land on the shore or share in any income.

Iradenergo gave no date for the study's results. The Mejlis budget committee has not been asked to consider a pilot. For now the winter load rests where it has for decades: on Toktogul, whose level the Herald will keep reporting as the drawdown continues.
